report:
### Findings Overview

Research does not definitively prove that a vegetarian diet inherently increases overall life expectancy compared to a diet containing meat. While vegetarians frequently enjoy better health outcomes, evidence suggests this is largely driven by broader healthy lifestyle habits rather than the exclusion of meat alone.

### Summary of Evidence

* **Evidence Supporting the Claim:** The Adventist Health Study-2 (AHS-2) observed a ~12% lower risk of all-cause mortality among vegetarians compared to non-vegetarians ([JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093)). Adventists generally abstain from alcohol and tobacco, making them a unique cohort.
* **Evidence Countering the Claim:** 
  * The British EPIC-Oxford study found no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians ([American Journal of Clinical Nutrition / ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916523238332)).
  * Australia’s large "45 and Up Study" similarly found no significant difference in all-cause mortality between vegetarians, semi-vegetarians, and regular meat eaters after controlling for variables such as age, smoking, alcohol use, and physical activity ([Preventive Medicine / ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091743516304479)).

### Conclusion

While vegetarians often have lower rates of specific conditions such as cardiovascular disease, their overall life expectancy is similar to that of health-conscious non-vegetarians. Overall lifestyle choices—such as maintaining a healthy weight, exercising, and avoiding smoking—appear to be stronger determinants of longevity than whether one consumes meat.

### Sources Cited

* EPIC-Oxford Mortality Study: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916523238332
* Australian 45 and Up Study: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091743516304479
